title: Baron Wilkins' club and Bricktop
summary: The band's arrival made Baron Wilkins' basement club the place to be.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I want to try and : -- get some background into the scene that you guys were on. Like Rex Stewart's book, Jazz Masters of the 1930's, he says that Baron Wilkins Club was one of the places you guys --

Yeah. Up in New York before -- he was the first. Baron Wilkins had a basement club. And he was -- it was a popular club. But the guys didn't really start hanging out there in a bunch until we came because he had never heard nobody like us. So the word spread and they come down there. The place was so packed they couldn't accommodate all the musicians trying to come in, you know. And one set rule that we had at that time, we were paid for entertaining people so we couldn't let just anybody walk in and play. We played Baron Wilkins, a little small basement club, packed with all the high powered people that eventually came to the Cotton Club, to the Kentucky Club, you know.
Baron Wilkins we had -- Ada Ward, Ada Brisktop got us the job there.
Oh, working at Baron Wilkins place?
Yeah, because she was hostess there. She got us this job in June and the business just tripled over night. The news spread and all the people from downtown started --

it got to be one of the clubs, they would come there, see. So all the musicians, our friends, they'd come in. But it was so small, we didn't have room to accommodate them guys, like six men playing. It couldn't do it. I mean, we -- he never turned them away but as far as playing, they come to listen. All of them come to listen, the white musicians, colored musicians.
